bmo-bmo1-2020-01.title: Examples, then work modulo 5
bmo-bmo1-2020-01.body:
**First part.** The values $p=5,\ 11,\ 101$ all work:
- $5,\ 7,\ 11,\ 13,\ 17$ are all prime;
- $11,\ 13,\ 17,\ 19,\ 23$ are all prime;
- $101,\ 103,\ 107,\ 109,\ 113$ are all prime (none is divisible by $2,3,5,7$, and $11^2>113$).

**Second part.** First, $q=5$ works: $5,7,11,13,17,19$ are all prime.

Now let $q$ be any prime with the property. Look at the five numbers
$$q,\quad q+6,\quad q+2,\quad q+8,\quad q+14 .$$
Their remainders on division by $5$ are $q,\ q+1,\ q+2,\ q+3,\ q+4 \pmod 5$, which are five consecutive residues, so they cover all residues modulo $5$. Hence one of these five numbers is divisible by $5$. Since it is prime, it **equals** $5$.

As $q\ge 2$, we have $q+6,\ q+8,\ q+14 \ge 8$, so either $q=5$ or $q+2=5$. If $q+2=5$ then $q=3$ and $q+6=9$ is not prime. Therefore $q=5$ is the only possibility, and it works. ∎

*Remark.* $5, 11, 101$ are in fact the only such $p$ below $200$ (the next is $1481$); a common slip is to treat $91=7\cdot 13$, $119=7\cdot17$, $143=11\cdot13$, $161=7\cdot 23$ or $169=13^2$ as prime.

bmo-bmo1-2020-02.title: Factorise and track parity
bmo-bmo1-2020-02.body:
The relation is $(2a_{n+1}-a_n)^2 = 1$, i.e. $2a_{n+1}-a_n=\pm1$, so
$$a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n+1}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n-1}{2}.$$
Conversely, any sequence in which every step is one of these two choices satisfies the relation. The sign may be chosen differently at each step.

**$a_1$ must be odd.** If $a_1$ is even, then $a_1\pm1$ is odd, so neither choice for $a_2$ is an integer, and no integer sequence exists.

**Every odd $a_1$ works.** Suppose $a_n$ is odd. The two candidates $\frac{a_n-1}{2}$ and $\frac{a_n+1}{2}$ are integers and differ by $1$, so exactly one of them is odd; choose $a_{n+1}$ to be that one. Starting from any odd $a_1$ and repeating this choice, we build (by induction) an infinite sequence of odd integers, each step satisfying the relation.

For example, $a_1=7$ gives $7, 3, 1, 1, 1,\dots$ and $a_1=-5$ gives $-5,-3,-1,-1,\dots$.

**Answer:** $a_1$ can be any odd integer. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2020-02.title: Work backwards from ±1
bmo-bmo1-2020-02.body:
As above, $a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n\pm1}{2}$, so $a_n = 2a_{n+1}\mp 1$ and $a_1$ is odd (an even $a_1$ gives no integer $a_2$).

If $|a_n|>1$ then $|a_{n+1}|\le \frac{|a_n|+1}{2}<|a_n|$, so the absolute values decrease until they reach $|a_k|\le 1$.

To see that every odd number occurs, use strong induction on $|a_1|$. For $a_1=\pm1$ the constant sequence $\pm1,\pm1,\dots$ works ($\frac{1+1}{2}=1$, $\frac{-1-1}{2}=-1$). If $a_1=2k+1$ with $|a_1|>1$, then the two allowed values of $a_2$ are $k$ and $k+1$; one of them is odd and has smaller absolute value than $a_1$, so by induction a valid sequence starts from it. Put $a_1$ in front of that sequence.

**Answer:** all odd integers. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2020-03.title: Common tangent at P and the alternate segment theorem
bmo-bmo1-2020-03.body:
Since $S_1, S_2$ have a common tangent not through $P$, they touch externally. Let the common tangent at $P$ meet $AB$ at $Y$.

**Step 1: $\angle APB=90^\circ$.** Tangent lengths from $Y$ give $YA=YP$ (circle $S_1$) and $YB=YP$ (circle $S_2$). Put $\gamma=\angle PAY=\angle YPA$ and $\delta=\angle PBY=\angle YPB$ (isosceles triangles $AYP$, $BYP$). Then $\angle APB=\gamma+\delta$, and the angle sum in triangle $APB$ gives $2\gamma+2\delta=180^\circ$, so
$$\gamma+\delta=90^\circ .$$

**Step 2: where $C$ and $D$ lie.**
- $S_1$ and $S_2$ lie on opposite sides of the tangent line at $P$, so $C$ and $D$ are on opposite sides of it and $P$ lies between $C$ and $D$ on line $CD$.
- The arc of $S_1$ on the same side of chord $AP$ as $Y$ lies inside triangle $AYP$ (it is cut off by the chord and the two tangents $YA$, $YP$), hence inside triangle $APB$. Since $C$ is outside triangle $APB$, $C$ lies on the other arc $AP$. Similarly $D$ lies on the arc $BP$ of $S_2$ on the side of chord $BP$ away from $Y$.

**Step 3: alternate segment theorem.** In $S_1$ the angle between tangent $AB$ and chord $AP$ equals the inscribed angle on the opposite arc:
$$\angle ACP=\angle PAB=\gamma .$$
Similarly in $S_2$: $\angle BDP=\angle PBA=\delta$.

**Step 4: the right angle.** Points $A$ and $B$ are on the same side of line $CD$. (Otherwise line $CD$ would cross segment $AB$ at a point $Q$. Points of segment $PQ$ lie in triangle $APB$, and points beyond $Q$ lie across $AB$ from both circles, so both $C$ and $D$ would have to lie on the ray from $P$ away from $Q$, contradicting that $P$ is between $C$ and $D$.) So rays $CA$ and $DB$ leave segment $CD$ on the same side, making angles $\angle ACD=\angle ACP=\gamma$ and $\angle BDC=\angle BDP=\delta$ with it. Since $\gamma+\delta=90^\circ<180^\circ$, the rays meet at a point $X$, and in triangle $XCD$
$$\angle CXD=180^\circ-\gamma-\delta=90^\circ .$$
Hence $AC\perp BD$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2020-03.title: Reduce to the diameters
bmo-bmo1-2020-03.body:
Let $O_1,O_2$ be the centres. Since $O_1P$ and $O_2P$ are both perpendicular to the common tangent at $P$, the points $O_1,P,O_2$ are collinear. Let $C'$ and $D'$ be the points diametrically opposite $P$ on $S_1$ and $S_2$; then $C',O_1,P,O_2,D'$ are collinear, so this is one allowed position of the line $CD$.

In quadrilateral $AO_1O_2B$ the angles at $A$ and $B$ are right angles (radius $\perp$ tangent), so $\angle AO_1O_2+\angle O_1O_2B=180^\circ$. These are exterior angles of the isosceles triangles $AO_1C'$ and $BO_2D'$, so $\angle AO_1O_2=2\angle O_1C'A$ and $\angle BO_2O_1=2\angle O_2D'B$. Therefore $\angle AC'P+\angle BD'P=90^\circ$.

For a general admissible line $CD$ through $P$: $C$ and $C'$ lie on the same arc $AP$ of $S_1$ (the one outside triangle $APB$), so $\angle ACP=\angle AC'P$ (angles in the same segment); similarly $\angle BDP=\angle BD'P$. Hence $\angle ACD+\angle BDC=90^\circ$, and as in the first solution lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet at a right angle. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2020-04.title: Track who can stand behind whom
bmo-bmo1-2020-04.body:
For $n>1$ let $p(n)$ be the smallest prime factor of $n$. The greatest proper divisor of $n$ is $m(n)=n/p(n)$, and penguin $n$ is inserted directly behind penguin $m(n)$. Two facts are used throughout:
- once two penguins are in the queue, their relative order never changes;
- a newcomer $k$ is placed **directly** behind $m(k)$, so it is behind penguin $x$ exactly when $m(k)=x$ or $m(k)$ is already behind $x$.

**(a)** *Claim:* at every stage, the penguins behind penguin $2$ are exactly the powers of two $4,8,16,\dots$ that have arrived.

By induction on arrivals. Penguin $3$ ($m=1$) goes in front of $2$. Suppose the claim holds before penguin $k$ arrives. By the second fact, $k$ goes behind $2$ iff $m(k)$ is $2$ or a power of two $\ge4$, i.e. iff $m(k)=2^i$ with $i\ge1$. If $k=2^{i+1}$ then $m(k)=2^i$. Conversely if $m(k)=2^i$ with $i\ge1$, then $k=p(k)\cdot 2^i$ is even, so $p(k)=2$ and $k=2^{i+1}$. This proves the claim.

So at the end the penguins behind $2$ are $4,8,\dots,1024$ — nine penguins. The number in front of penguin $2$ is $2019-1-9=\mathbf{2009}$.

**(b) Just behind 33.** The penguin directly behind $33$ changes only when a newcomer $k$ has $m(k)=33$ (an insertion anywhere else does not separate $33$ from its follower). Then $k=33\,p(k)$ with $p(k)\le 3$ (the smallest prime factor of $k$ is at most that of $33$), so $k\in\{66,99\}$. Penguin $66$ arrives first and stands behind $33$; then $99$ is inserted directly behind $33$. So the penguin just behind $33$ is $\mathbf{99}$.

**Just in front of 33.** When $33$ arrives it stands directly behind $11$. The penguin $x$ directly in front of $33$ changes only when a newcomer $k$ with $m(k)=x$ arrives; then $k$ becomes the new $x$.
- $x=11$ (from time $33$): newcomers with $m(k)=11$ are $11p$ with prime $p\le 11$, i.e. $22,33,55,77,121$. The first after $33$ is $55$.
- $x=55$: $m(k)=55$ means $k=55p$, $p\le5$: $110,165,275$. First after $55$: $110$.
- $x=110$: $m(k)=110$ needs $p\le2$, so $k=220$; likewise $220\to440\to880\to1760$, and the next would be $3520>2019$.

So the penguin just in front of $33$ is $\mathbf{1760}$.

**Answer:** (a) $2009$; (b) $1760$ in front and $99$ behind. ∎

*(A direct simulation of all 2019 arrivals confirms these numbers.)*

bmo-bmo1-2020-05.title: Construction plus two invariants
bmo-bmo1-2020-05.body:
Number the children $1,\dots,6$ around the table, child $1$ starting with the sweets. Child $i$'s neighbours are $i\pm1$ and the child opposite is $i+3$ (indices mod 6). Note that all three recipients of a move by child $i$ have the opposite parity to $i$.

**Sufficiency: $n=28k$ works.**
1. Child $1$ makes $7k$ moves. Before the $j$-th of these child $1$ has $28k-4(j-1)\ge 4$ sweets, so each move is legal. Afterwards child $1$ has $0$, children $2,4,6$ have $7k$ each, children $3,5$ have $0$.
2. Each of children $2,4,6$ now makes $k$ moves. Even children never give to each other, so each even child only loses sweets through its own moves and has at least $7k-4(k-1)\ge4$ before each move. Afterwards each even child has $7k-4k=3k$, and each odd child received one sweet from each move of an even child: $3k$ sweets.

Everybody has $3k$, so the arrangement is perfect.

**Necessity.** Let $O$ and $E$ be the total numbers of sweets held by odd- and even-numbered children.
- A move by an odd child lowers $O$ by $4$ and raises $E$ by $3$; a move by an even child does the reverse. So every move changes $O-E$ by exactly $\pm7$. Initially $O-E=n$; in an equal final position $O-E=0$. Hence $7\mid n$.
- Let $D$ = (sweets of child 1) $-$ (sweets of child 3). A move by child $1$ changes $D$ by $-4$ (child $1$ gives to $2,6,4$); a move by child $3$ changes it by $+4$. Child $2$ gives to $1,3,5$; child $4$ to $3,5,1$; child $6$ to $5,1,3$ — each of these raises both child $1$ and child $3$ by one or neither (child $5$ gives to $4,6,2$), so $D$ is unchanged. Thus $D \bmod 4$ is invariant. Initially $D=n$, finally $D=0$, so $4\mid n$.

Since $\gcd(4,7)=1$, $28\mid n$.

**Answer:** the initial arrangement is perfect exactly when $n$ is a multiple of $28$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2020-05.title: Count the moves (algebra)
bmo-bmo1-2020-05.body:
Suppose a successful sequence exists in which children $1,\dots,6$ make $a,b,c,d,e,f$ moves. Child $i$ ends with (initial sweets) $-4\cdot$(own moves) $+$ (moves made by its three opposite-parity partners):
$$\begin{array}{ll}
\text{child }1: & n+b+d+f-4a\\
\text{child }2,4,6: & a+c+e-4b,\quad a+c+e-4d,\quad a+c+e-4f\\
\text{child }3,5: & b+d+f-4c,\quad b+d+f-4e
\end{array}$$
Equating children $2,4,6$ gives $b=d=f$. Equating children $3,5$ gives $c=e$, and equating children $1$ and $3$ gives $n=4(a-c)$. Equating children $2$ and $3$: $a+2c-4b=3b-4c$, so $a=7b-6c$. Then $n=4(7b-6c-c)=28(b-c)$, a multiple of $28$.

Together with the construction from the first solution ($n=28k$ works), the answer is: **all positive multiples of $28$**. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2020-06.title: Shift along the diagonal, then a one-variable recurrence
bmo-bmo1-2020-06.body:
Call the three expressions $L$, $M$, $R$.

**Step 1: $f(m+1,n+1)=f(m,n)+1$.** Write $L=M$ for $(m,n)$ and for $(m+1,n+1)$:
$$2f(m,n)=f(m-n,n-m)+m+n,\qquad 2f(m+1,n+1)=f(m-n,n-m)+m+n+2 .$$
Subtracting gives $f(m+1,n+1)=f(m,n)+1$. Applying this repeatedly (forwards and backwards) gives, for all $m,n$,
$$f(m,n)=f(m-n,0)+n. \tag{1}$$

**Step 2: a recurrence for $g(p)=f(p,0)$.** Take $(m,n)=(p,0)$ in $L=R$ and use (1) on $f(p,1)=f(p-1,0)+1$:
$$2g(p)=g(p+1)+\bigl(g(p-1)+1\bigr)-1=g(p+1)+g(p-1).$$
So $g(p+1)-g(p)=g(p)-g(p-1)$ for all $p$: the differences are constant, and $g(p)=g(0)+bp$ where $b=g(1)-g(0)$ is an integer.

Taking $m=n=0$ in $L=M$ gives $2f(0,0)=f(0,0)$, so $g(0)=0$ and $g(p)=bp$. By (1),
$$f(m,n)=b(m-n)+n .$$

**Step 3: these all work.** For $f(m,n)=b(m-n)+n$:
- $L=2b(m-n)+2n$;
- $M=f(m-n,n-m)+m+n=b(2m-2n)+(n-m)+m+n=2b(m-n)+2n$;
- $R=[b(m+1-n)+n]+[b(m-n-1)+n+1]-1=2b(m-n)+2n$.

All three agree, and the values are integers.

**Answer:** the good functions are exactly $f(m,n)=(b+1)m-bn$ with $b\in\mathbb Z$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2020-06.title: Reduce to the anti-diagonal
bmo-bmo1-2020-06.body:
Let $g(k)=f(k,-k)$. From $L=M$, $f(m,n)=\tfrac12\bigl(g(m-n)+m+n\bigr)$ for all $m,n$; in particular ($m=n=0$) $g(0)=0$.

Substitute this into $L=R$ with $n=0$:
$$g(m)+m=\tfrac12\bigl(g(m+1)+m+1\bigr)+\tfrac12\bigl(g(m-1)+m+1\bigr)-1,$$
which simplifies to $2g(m)=g(m+1)+g(m-1)$. So $g$ is linear: $g(m)=am$ with $a=g(1)$, and
$$f(m,n)=\tfrac12\bigl((1+a)m+(1-a)n\bigr).$$
Since $f(1,0)=\frac{1+a}{2}$ must be an integer, $a$ is odd, say $a=2b+1$, giving $f(m,n)=(b+1)m-bn$. These functions satisfy all the equations (checked in the first solution). ∎
